title: Cloud Data Science and Scalable Infrastructure
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Cloud Data Science and Scalable Infrastructure ##### The ₹4.1 lakh notebook A four-person data team at an edtech company in Hyderabad had a very good week in March. They got approval for cloud infrastructure, spun up a SageMaker notebook instance on a `ml.p3.2xlarge` — one NVIDIA V100, about ₹280 an hour in the Mumbai region — and fine-tuned a recommendation model. It worked. Everyone was pleased. Then Holi happened, and then a long weekend, and then a sprint that pulled everyone onto a different problem. The notebook instance stayed running for fifty-one days. Nobody had attached a budget alert, because nobody had known that budget alerts existed. Finance found it in the May invoice: ₹4,12,000 for a GPU that had been idle since the third week of March, plus another ₹38,000 for an EBS volume attached to a stopped instance that they had assumed cost nothing. The technical lesson is small — stop your instances. The real lesson is bigger, and it is what today is about. **Cloud infrastructure is not a faster laptop. It is a different discipline**, where every resource has a meter attached, every permission is a security decision, and the architecture you sketch on a whiteboard becomes a line item on a bill. A data scientist who can train a model but cannot reason about IAM roles, storage tiers, and cost is a data scientist whose work stays on their laptop. ##### The layer cake: what the cloud actually gives you Strip away the 200 service names and every cloud provider offers you the same five things. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Object Storage
S3 / GCS / ADLS
cheap, infinite, durable"] --> B["Compute
VMs, containers, serverless
metered by the second"] A --> C["Managed Warehouse
BigQuery / Redshift / Snowflake
SQL over the lake"] B --> D["Managed ML Platform
SageMaker / Vertex AI
notebooks, training, endpoints"] C --> D D --> E["Serving
real-time endpoint or batch job"] F["IAM & Networking
who can touch what"] -.governs.-> A F -.governs.-> B F -.governs.-> C F -.governs.-> D G["Billing & Budgets
the meter on everything"] -.measures.-> B G -.measures.-> C G -.measures.-> D ``` Everything you build sits somewhere on this cake. Let's take the layers in order. ##### Object storage and the data lake S3, Google Cloud Storage, and Azure Data Lake Storage are the foundation. They are not filesystems — they are key-value stores where the key looks like a path and the value is a blob. This distinction matters: there are no real directories (the "folders" you see are a prefix convention), renaming is a copy plus delete, and appending to an object is not a thing. What you get in exchange is remarkable: eleven nines of durability, effectively unlimited capacity, and a price of roughly ₹2 per GB per month for standard storage. That cheapness is what makes the **data lake** pattern viable — dump everything in raw form, decide what it means later. The organising conventions that separate a lake from a swamp: ``` s3://company-datalake/ ├── bronze/ # raw, immutable, exactly as received │ └── source=crm/dt=2026-07-28/part-0000.json.gz ├── silver/ # cleaned, typed, deduplicated │ └── customers/dt=2026-07-28/part-0000.parquet └── gold/ # business-ready aggregates & features └── churn_features/dt=2026-07-28/part-0000.parquet ``` Three things to internalise: - **Partition by date in the key prefix** (`dt=2026-07-28/`). Query engines use this for partition pruning — a query for July reads July's objects and skips the rest of the year. This alone routinely cuts scan costs by 90%+. - **Store Parquet, not CSV.** Columnar layout plus compression means you read only the columns you need, and warehouses that bill by bytes scanned will bill you a fraction as much. - **Use lifecycle policies.** Move objects older than 90 days to infrequent-access, older than a year to archive tiers. A one-line policy can cut storage cost by 70% on cold data. ##### Managed warehouses: SQL without servers BigQuery, Redshift, and Snowflake all let you run SQL over enormous datasets without managing a database. They differ mainly in their billing model, and the billing model determines how you should work. | | Pricing model | Watch out for | Best fit | |---|---|---|---| | **BigQuery** | Per TB scanned (on-demand) or slot reservations | `SELECT *` on a wide table costs real money every single time | Bursty, unpredictable analytical workloads | | **Snowflake** | Per second of warehouse uptime, by warehouse size | Warehouses left running with auto-suspend disabled | Mixed workloads, multi-cloud, easy scaling | | **Redshift** | Provisioned cluster hours, or Serverless RPU-hours | Idle clusters billing 24/7; distribution key mistakes | Steady, predictable AWS-native workloads | A concrete BigQuery habit worth building: always check the estimated bytes before running. The console shows it in the top-right; from Python: ```python from google.cloud import bigquery client = bigquery.Client(project="edtech-analytics") sql = """ SELECT state, course_category, COUNT(DISTINCT learner_id) AS learners, ROUND(AVG(completion_pct), 2) AS avg_completion FROM `edtech-analytics.gold.enrollments` WHERE enrolment_date BETWEEN '2026-04-01' AND '2026-06-30' AND country = 'IN' GROUP BY state, course_category ORDER BY learners DESC """ # Dry run first: costs nothing, tells you what the real run will scan. dry = client.query(sql, job_config=bigquery.QueryJobConfig(dry_run=True)) gb = dry.total_bytes_processed / 1e9 print(f"This query will scan {gb:.2f} GB (~₹{gb * 0.52:.2f})") if gb < 50: df = client.query(sql).to_dataframe() ``` That dry-run guard, wrapped in a helper function, is the difference between a team that experiments freely and a team that gets its BigQuery access revoked. ##### Managed compute and ML platforms The value proposition of SageMaker or Vertex AI is that they handle the undifferentiated parts: provisioning a GPU box, installing CUDA, pulling your data, running your script, shutting the box down, and storing the artifact. The key mental shift is from **notebooks** to **jobs**. A notebook instance is a machine you rent by the hour and must remember to stop. A training job is a machine that is created, used, and destroyed automatically. The Hyderabad team's ₹4.1 lakh mistake is structurally impossible with training jobs. ```python import sagemaker from sagemaker.sklearn.estimator import SKLearn session = sagemaker.Session() role = "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/EdtechSageMakerExecutionRole" estimator = SKLearn( entry_point="train.py", source_dir="src/", role=role, instance_type="ml.m5.2xlarge", # CPU: ~₹34/hr. Use GPU only if you need it. instance_count=1, framework_version="1.2-1", py_version="py3", use_spot_instances=True, # up to 70% cheaper max_run=3600, # hard kill after 1 hour max_wait=7200, # spot wait budget hyperparameters={"n_estimators": 400, "max_depth": 12}, output_path="s3://company-datalake/models/churn/", tags=[ {"Key": "team", "Value": "data-science"}, {"Key": "project", "Value": "churn-v3"}, {"Key": "env", "Value": "dev"}, ], ) estimator.fit({"train": "s3://company-datalake/gold/churn_features/train/", "validation": "s3://company-datalake/gold/churn_features/val/"}) predictor = estimator.deploy( initial_instance_count=1, instance_type="ml.m5.large", endpoint_name="churn-v3-prod", ) ``` Four cost controls are hiding in that block, and all four are habits worth making automatic: - **`use_spot_instances=True`** — spare capacity at a 60–70% discount. It can be reclaimed mid-run, so checkpoint your training loop, but for most jobs under two hours the risk is small and the saving is large. - **`max_run`** — a hard timeout. A runaway job dies instead of billing overnight. - **CPU by default.** A GPU is ~8× the price. Gradient-boosted trees and scikit-learn models get nothing from it. - **Tags.** Every resource tagged with team, project, and environment. Without tags, your cloud bill is one enormous unattributable number and nobody can be accountable for it. ##### Infrastructure basics you cannot skip **IAM** is the permission system, and it is where the security incidents live. Three concepts: - **Principal** — who is acting (a user, or more often a *role* assumed by a service). - **Policy** — a JSON document listing allowed actions on which resources. - **Least privilege** — grant only what is needed. `s3:GetObject` on `arn:aws:s3:::company-datalake/gold/churn_features/*`, not `s3:*` on `*`. The pattern that matters most in practice: **services should assume roles, humans should not hold long-lived keys.** If your training script has an access key hardcoded in it, you have already lost. Use the instance's attached role and let the SDK pick up credentials automatically. ```json { "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:ListBucket"], "Resource": [ "arn:aws:s3:::company-datalake", "arn:aws:s3:::company-datalake/gold/churn_features/*" ] }, { "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:PutObject"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::company-datalake/models/churn/*" } ] } ``` **VMs vs containers vs serverless** is a spectrum of how much you manage: | | You manage | Startup | Bills for | Good for | |---|---|---|---|---| | VM (EC2/Compute Engine) | OS, runtime, deps, scaling | ~60s | Whole instance-hours | Long-running, custom environments | | Container (ECS/GKE/Cloud Run) | Image contents only | ~5–20s | Container runtime | Reproducible services, most ML APIs | | Serverless (Lambda/Cloud Functions) | Function code only | ~100ms–3s | Per invocation + ms | Spiky, short, event-driven work | For model serving, containers are the sweet spot — which is exactly why Day 36's FastAPI-in-Docker service translates directly to Cloud Run or ECS with no code change. **Autoscaling** adjusts capacity to load. Set a minimum of 1 (or 0 if cold starts are acceptable), a maximum that caps your worst-case bill, and a target metric — usually CPU utilisation around 60% or requests-per-instance. The maximum is a cost control, not just a capacity setting; without it a traffic spike or a retry storm becomes a five-figure bill. ##### Cost management as an engineering practice Cost is a non-functional requirement, like latency. Treat it that way. - **Budget alerts on day zero.** Before you launch anything, create a budget with alerts at 50%, 80%, and 100% of your monthly ceiling, emailed to a real person. This is a two-minute task that would have saved the Hyderabad team ₹4 lakh. - **Tag everything**, then use cost allocation reports to see spend by project. - **Right-size, then re-check.** Start smaller than you think you need and scale up on evidence. - **Auto-stop notebooks.** SageMaker lifecycle configs and Vertex AI idle shutdown will kill an idle instance after N minutes. Enable them organisation-wide. - **Prefer batch to real-time.** A daily batch prediction job writing to a table costs a tiny fraction of an always-on endpoint. Only pay for real-time inference when the product genuinely needs it. - **Watch egress.** Moving data *out* of a cloud region is billed; moving it in is usually free. Keep compute in the same region as storage — for Indian workloads, typically `ap-south-1` (Mumbai), which also helps with latency and with data-residency expectations under the DPDP Act 2023. ##### Security fundamentals - **Encryption at rest** — on by default in modern S3/GCS. Use customer-managed keys when compliance requires it. - **Encryption in transit** — TLS everywhere, no exceptions. - **Never commit credentials.** Use Secrets Manager or the platform's secret store; scan your repos with `gitleaks` in CI. - **Block public bucket access** at the account level. The single most common cloud data breach is a misconfigured public bucket. - **PII handling** — under India's DPDP Act 2023 you need a lawful basis for processing personal data, and users have rights to correction and erasure. Practically: keep PII in a separate, tightly-scoped bucket prefix, pseudonymise identifiers in your feature store, and log who accessed what via CloudTrail. - **VPC and private endpoints** — keep training traffic off the public internet where you can. ##### Common mistakes - Launching a GPU instance for a workload that has no GPU-accelerated step. - Forgetting that stopped instances still bill for attached storage. - Using `SELECT *` against a per-TB-scanned warehouse. - Granting `AdministratorAccess` to a service role "just to unblock things," then never revoking it. - Storing raw CSV in the lake and re-parsing it on every single query. - Building in one region and storing data in another, then paying egress on every read. - No budget alerts, so the first signal is the invoice. - Untagged resources, making cost attribution impossible after the fact. - Deploying an always-on real-time endpoint for a batch use case. - Treating the cloud console as the source of truth instead of infrastructure-as-code, so nothing is reproducible. ##### Hands-on: build the smallest complete thing Your practical task is deliberately end-to-end at tiny scale: create a bucket, upload a dataset, query it from a managed warehouse or cloud notebook, and set a budget alert. Do the budget alert **first**. Make it a reflex — bucket, data, query, alert, in that order, every time you touch a new project. The mini project scales that into a real workflow: data in object storage, training on managed compute, model behind a managed endpoint, with the IAM roles and estimated cost written down. The documentation is not busywork — writing "this role can read `gold/` and write `models/`, nothing else" is how you discover you granted `s3:*`. And estimating cost before you build is how you discover that the endpoint you were about to deploy costs ₹19,000 a month to serve forty predictions a day. The assignment asks for an architecture diagram of a batch prediction pipeline with storage, compute, orchestration, and security controls labelled, plus your cost-control reasoning. Draw it in Mermaid so it lives in your repo's README. Being able to defend "we chose scheduled batch on spot instances over a real-time endpoint because the business consumes predictions once a day, which cuts cost by 94%" is a senior-level answer, and it is the kind of thing interviewers remember. ##### Key takeaways - The cloud is five layers — **object storage, compute, warehouse, managed ML, and the IAM/billing controls that govern them** — and almost every architecture is a specific arrangement of those five. - **Object storage is the foundation**: partition by date, store Parquet, use lifecycle policies, and organise bronze/silver/gold. - **Prefer ephemeral jobs to long-lived notebooks**, spot instances to on-demand, CPU to GPU, and batch to real-time unless the product truly needs otherwise. - **IAM least privilege and tagged resources are engineering practices**, not paperwork — they prevent both breaches and unattributable bills. - **Set budget alerts before you provision anything.** Cost is a design constraint you own, not a surprise finance discovers eight weeks later.
